newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombians plumb new depths of pessimism - poll.
newsitem.headline: Colombians plumb new depths of pessimism - poll.

text.p: Colombians are more pessimistic than ever about their violent and crisis-torn nation, according to a poll published on Sunday in Semana, the country's leading news magazine.

The Gallup poll, conducted on Oct. 31, showed that an overwhelming 86 percent of Colombians thought their country was going from bad to worse, while 92 percent believed it was losing the battle with seemingly runaway levels of corruption.

The survey also showed that 92 percent of Colombians thought the country's guerrilla war against leftist rebels was going badly and 85 percent believed its law and order situation was being handled badly.

President Ernesto Samper, who has been dogged by charges that he used drug money to win election in 1994, has said repeatedly that his government should be credited with leading a sweeping crackdown on cocaine kingpins since taking office.
But 80 percent of survey respondents said they thought that Colombia was not winning its battle against drugs.
Not surprisingly, given the political crisis stemming from Samper's alleged drug ties, a full 88 percent also said they thought Colombia's image abroad was getting worse.

Only 64 percent described themselves as happy or content compared to 86 percent in a Gallup survey conducted in April 1992. Only six percent said they had confidence in the country's political parties to lead it out of its current mess.
Trust in institutions like the military, and even the church in the largely Roman Catholic country, was down sharply compared to a similar Gallup poll conducted in December 1995.
Only 57 percent of respondents said they trusted the church, compared to 71 percent in December 1995. And just 41 percent said they had faith in the military, as opposed to 61 percent 11 months ago.
"This is the highest percentage of collective pessimism since we began carrying out this type of survey in Colombia," Jorge Londono, the head of the Gallup Colombia, told Semana.
He said the percentage was higher even than the level of pessimism shown in a poll conducted in Bosnia in late 1994.
No margin of error was given for the poll and Londono was unavailable for comment on its methodology.
